source: Stevenson et al. (2022) Putting GPT-3's Creativity to the (Alternative Uses) Test
finding: First psychological AUT test of an LLM. Humans got higher originality and surprise ratings and larger semantic distance. GPT-3 got higher utility ratings.
numbers: Humans: 42 students, 823 Dutch responses (774 valid); GPT-3 davinci-002: 144 runs, 781 valid responses; objects book, fork, tin can. Originality beta=.17 (p=.004), surprise beta=.14 (p=.050), semantic distance beta=.10 (p<.001), utility beta=-.55 (p<.001).
limits: Small student sample, translated Dutch, GPT-3 prompt and temperature (.65-.80) tuned by Monte Carlo runs but humans got minimal instructions. Authors suspect creativity tests were in the training data.
agent_relevance: Old model. Shows the originality versus utility axis must be measured together in open mode.

source: Stevenson et al. (2022) Putting GPT-3's Creativity to the (Alternative Uses) Test
finding: Originality and utility trade off in both groups. Raters were blinded after cleaning surface cues such as numbering and 'Use a X to'.
numbers: Originality-utility correlation r=-.56 (humans) and r=-.61 (GPT-3). ICC after cleaning: originality .78, utility .70, surprise .79 (before cleaning .57, .68, .67).
limits: Rating needed prior removal of style tells, so unblinded raters would be biased.
agent_relevance: Any judge of our open-mode output must score both originality and usefulness, with style stripped, or it rewards the wrong thing.

source: Stevenson et al. (2022) Putting GPT-3's Creativity to the (Alternative Uses) Test
finding: Flexibility (categories divided by responses) was higher in humans, but GPT-3 flexibility varied more across runs and was unrelated to temperature.
numbers: Humans higher, F(1,85)=5.53, p=.021; GPT-3 flexibility vs temperature r=.04, p=.80.
limits: Categories coded by three judges, one per object; tin can only.
agent_relevance: Temperature does not buy conceptual switching. Switching needs an explicit mechanism (operator), not a sampling knob.

source: Stevenson et al. (2022) Putting GPT-3's Creativity to the (Alternative Uses) Test
finding: Authors flag that the AUT may not measure creativity at all, citing Runco 2008 'divergent thinking is not synonymous with creativity'.
limits: Argument only.
agent_relevance: Divergent-thinking scores are a proxy. Our open-mode metric should be treated as a proxy as well.

source: Nath, Dayan and Stevenson (2024) Characterising the Creative Process in Humans and Large Language Models
finding: Automated jump signal from sentence-embedding similarity between successive AUT answers. Humans show persistent (deep in few categories) and flexible (many switches) paths to creativity with similar scores.
numbers: Reliability: test-retest of jump counts r=0.42 (N=81 humans, brick vs paperclip). Human clusters on AUT: persistent 7-12 jumps, flexible 15-18, mixed 12-16. Human originality did not differ between persistent and flexible clusters (p>0.05).
limits: Human data are undergraduates in Amsterdam; jump signal for the validity check was hand-coded by first author.
agent_relevance: Gives a cheap code-level process metric (jump count) for open mode. Both depth and breadth are valid routes, so do not force switching on every step (fits G1).

source: Nath, Dayan and Stevenson (2024) Characterising the Creative Process in Humans and Large Language Models
finding: LLMs match humans on jump count on the AUT, but are far more persistent than humans on verbal fluency (animals). Their jumping is less consistent across items.
numbers: LLM test-retest r=0.22 (CI .12-.31) vs humans 0.42. AUT jumps: LLM vs human p>0.05; VFT: LLMs more persistent, p<0.001. Models tested include GPT, Claude, PaLM, Llama, Gemini, Mistral, NousResearch, Upstage SOLAR.
limits: Cluster assignment of models changed between brick and paperclip.
agent_relevance: LLM search style is unstable across prompts. An agent should measure its own jump profile rather than assume it.

source: Nath, Dayan and Stevenson (2024) Characterising the Creative Process in Humans and Large Language Models
finding: For LLMs, flexible response sequences had higher originality; for humans, no such link. Temperature did not change cluster assignment on the AUT.
numbers: LLM mean originality higher in flexible cluster (p<0.01) and predicts jump count (p<=0.01); LLMs scored higher mean originality than humans on both AUTs (p<0.001). Temperature on AUT jumps p>0.05.
limits: Originality ratings ignore utility.
agent_relevance: Strong hint that for LLMs, forced category switching raises originality (breadth route). Testable lever for open mode.

source: Haase and Hanel (2023) Artificial muses: generative AI chatbots have risen to human-level creativity
finding: On the AUT, chatbots were not different from humans in mean originality. A minority of humans beat the best chatbot on each prompt.
numbers: N=100 humans (Prolific, USA), 5 chatbots (ChatGPT-3, Alpa, Copy.ai, Studio, YouChat), GPT-4 added later; 5 objects. Mixed model human-rated B=-0.21, SE=0.15, p=.218; AI-rated B=-0.18, p=.241. Number of humans above the best chatbot: 42 (human ratings) and 52 (AI ratings) for pants; 32.8 on average over prompts; 9.4% of humans beat GPT-4 overall (abstract).
limits: Chatbot n=5 versus humans n=100; chatbots were prompted several times and produced 2-3 times more ideas; repeated prompting and 'more like this' changes the sampling.
agent_relevance: Best-of-many sampling gives parity with the average human. The edge of the best human is the real bar.

source: Haase and Hanel (2023) Artificial muses: generative AI chatbots have risen to human-level creativity
finding: Rater reliability was high and a trained scoring AI agreed with human raters. Fluency and originality were nearly unrelated.
numbers: Six raters ICC .85-.94; human-vs-AI rater r=.78-.94 (p<.0001); fluency vs originality r=-.28 to .26.
limits: Fluency scoring is trivial for LLMs, so only originality is informative.
agent_relevance: A trained scorer can stand in for raters in group-level tests (OCS-style).

source: Koivisto and Grassini (2023) Best humans still outperform artificial intelligence in a creative divergent thinking task
finding: On the AUT, three chatbots beat the average human on semantic distance and on human ratings. The best human responses matched or exceeded the best AI ones.
numbers: N=256 humans; ChatGPT-3, ChatGPT-4, Copy.ai; objects rope, box, pencil, candle. Mean semantic distance AI>human B=0.049 (p<.001); max score B=0.027 (p=.003). Subjective mean B=0.453; max B=0.403 (both p<.001), controlling for fluency. Group effect on mean semantic distance: F(3,273)=9.0, p<.001 (ChatGPT3 p=.021, ChatGPT4 p<.001 vs humans).
limits: Max-score group differences were not significant after multiple-comparison correction (all p>.223). Humans had low-scoring tails: in 7% of trials, human max rating <2; AI never.
agent_relevance: Gain comes from removing poor ideas (floor), not raising the ceiling. Means up; peak not.

source: Koivisto and Grassini (2023) Best humans still outperform artificial intelligence in a creative divergent thinking task
finding: Fluency acts as a confound: more responses lower the mean originality but raise the max.
numbers: Fluency covariate: mean semantic distance B=-0.012 (p<.001), max B=+0.011 (p<.001); subjective mean B=-0.088, max B=+0.139.
agent_relevance: Report mean and max of originality together, always with the response count. Open-mode metric should be max-of-N and mean-of-N.

source: Koivisto and Grassini (2023) Best humans still outperform artificial intelligence in a creative divergent thinking task
finding: Correlation of semantic distance with human subjective ratings is moderate.
agent_relevance: Semantic distance is a partial proxy; do not use alone.

source: Koivisto and Grassini (2023) Best humans still outperform artificial intelligence in a creative divergent thinking task
finding: Authors explain the human lag by weak executive control (goal maintenance, inhibition of near concepts, switching), per controlled-attention accounts of creativity.
limits: Interpretation, not tested.
agent_relevance: Maps onto an agent: hold the goal, suppress the first obvious idea, switch category. Operators for open mode.

source: Hubert, Awa and Zabelina (2024) The current state of artificial intelligence generative language models is more creative than humans on divergent thinking tasks
finding: GPT-4 beat humans on three divergent tasks (AUT, Consequences, Divergent Association) when fluency was matched afterwards.
numbers: N=151 humans vs GPT-4; AUT items rope, fork. AUT fluency matched: human M=6.94 vs GPT-4 M=7.01. Elaboration: GPT-4 M=15.45 vs human M=3.38, t(602)=28.57. Originality (semantic distance, OCS GloVe): group F(1,600)=622.10, eta2=.51, p<.001.
limits: Fluency matched post hoc by downsampling (GPT-4 generated more, then cut). The reported ANOVA statistics for the AUT and Consequences tasks are identical (F=622.10, 584.50, 113.80), which looks like a copy error. Elaboration by word count favours verbose LLM.
agent_relevance: Treat the huge effect with caution: post hoc matching, semantic distance, and word count all favour LLM style.

source: Review in PMC13608707 (2026) Evaluation of large language models as tools, models and partners in creative thinking research (GCA framework)
finding: Review of LLM divergent-thinking studies (Jan 2018 to Jun 2026): LLMs beat the average human, but the advantage depends on how fluency is controlled and does not hold against top humans.
numbers: Hedges g for LLM over average human 0.52 to 2.61 over four independent comparisons; largest from post hoc fluency matching (Hubert 2024), moderate from prospective matching (Koivisto 2023) and figural flexibility, smallest from 100,000-human DAT (g 0.52). Peak comparisons: g=-0.88 against top 50% of humans on DAT; g=-1.31 on figural subjective creativity.
limits: Selective narrative review; effect sizes recomputed by the authors, not pooled; thresholds are 'provisional heuristics'.
agent_relevance: Use a ladder of comparisons (average, top half, top decile). Beating the mean is cheap.

source: Review in PMC13608707 (2026) Evaluation of large language models as tools, models and partners in creative thinking research (GCA framework)
finding: Automated scoring with LLMs is good at group level but not for individuals, and weaker outside English.
numbers: Organisciak 2023: LLM-based scoring ICC above 0.80 versus expert ratings; selected studies ICC>=0.80 and r>=0.70. Guo 2024: Chinese vs American students scalar invariance for fluency but only partial for originality.
limits: Reported ICC forms differ and are often unspecified.
agent_relevance: An LLM judge for open mode should be used for means over many items, never to rank single outputs (matches G5).

source: Review in PMC13608707 (2026) Evaluation of large language models as tools, models and partners in creative thinking research (GCA framework)
finding: Review argues LLMs model only the associative part of creativity, not insight, incubation or conscious evaluation. Likelihood training favours typical output (novelty-typicality trade-off).
numbers: Structural claim; no single number.
limits: Mechanism arguments are mostly hypotheses.
agent_relevance: Supports using code-level selection and explicit novelty pressure, not trusting free sampling.

source: Review in PMC13608707 (2026) Evaluation of large language models as tools, models and partners in creative thinking research (GCA framework)
finding: Secondary account of the founding theory: Guilford (1950) separates divergent and convergent thinking; Mednick (1962) places individual differences in the organisation of semantic memory; Geneplore alternates generation and exploration (Finke 1992); Runco and Jaeger (2012) give the standard definition of novel plus useful.
limits: Not primary. Guilford 1950/1967, Mednick 1962 and Runco 2008 were not opened by me this session.
agent_relevance: Divergent output is a stage, not the whole of creativity; pair it with an evaluation stage.

source: Bellemare-Pepin et al. (2024/2026) Divergent creativity in humans and large language models
finding: On the Divergent Association Task (name 10 unrelated words) GPT-4 beat the average of 100,000 humans, but the top human decile, quartile and upper half beat every model tested.
numbers: Human reference N=100,000; LLM bars each n=500 generations. GPT-4 significantly above human mean; Gemini Pro indistinguishable; GPT-4-turbo lower than GPT-4. GPT-4 temperature 1.5 gave mean DAT 85.6, above 72% of human scores. Vs top 50% of humans in review: g=-0.88.
limits: DAT is a narrow word task. Newer GPT-4 versions were not consistently better. Models with low scores often failed to follow instructions.
agent_relevance: The ceiling is a human-best ceiling. Temperature helps on this task.

source: Bellemare-Pepin et al. (2024/2026) Divergent creativity in humans and large language models
finding: Output of the best model is highly repetitive across runs. Prompt strategy changed scores.
numbers: GPT-4: 70% of word sets contain 'microscope', 60% 'elephant'; GPT-4-turbo: 'ocean' in more than 90% of sets; humans' most common word car 1.4%, dog 1.2%. Strategy prompts (meaning opposition, thesaurus, etymology): all differences significant except thesaurus vs basic; etymology beat basic prompt for both GPT-3.5 and GPT-4.
limits: Strategy effect tested on DAT only.
agent_relevance: Mode collapse inside one model: raising the mean can still give the same few answers. Check across runs, not within one run.

source: Homogeneity study (2026) Large language models are homogeneously creative (PMC13010328)
finding: Across 22 LLMs and 102 humans on AUT, Forward Flow and DAT, LLM responses are much more alike than human responses even with equal originality.
numbers: Originality: AUT LLM 0.711 vs human 0.696 (d=0.1); FF 0.603 vs 0.637 (humans higher, d=0.52); DAT 0.801 vs 0.753. Variability across responses: AUT 0.459 vs 0.699 (d=1.8, t(308)=12.6); FF 0.518 vs 0.642 (d=0.87); DAT 0.632 vs 0.791 (d=1.1).
limits: Embedding-based semantic metrics; small human sample; LLM overlap partly lexical (shared words).
agent_relevance: Average originality hides homogeneity. Open mode must measure spread across samples, and ensembles of different models do not give independent ideas (consistent with G4).

source: Anderson, Shah and Kreminski (2024) Homogenization effects of large language models on human creative ideation
finding: Human users of ChatGPT generated ideas that were more similar to each other across users than users of a card-deck tool (Oblique Strategies), though no more similar within one person.
numbers: N=36 within-subject. Group-level distance from mean embedding: ChatGPT M=.24 vs OS M=.28, t(32)=2.154, p=.038, d=.47. Within-person: .65 vs .66, p=.352, d=.12. Categories hit: 8.58 vs 6.77, p=.001, d=.54. Elaboration word count 8.25 vs 6.46. Unique ideas 0.74 vs 0.97, p=.108. Sense of responsibility lower with ChatGPT, d=.67, p=.003.
limits: Small sample, one task, one tool, ChatGPT in early 2024.
agent_relevance: Support for a rule: single-model idea pools collapse at group level even when each run looks diverse.

source: Beaty and Johnson (2021) Automating creativity assessment with SemDis
finding: Semantic distance from five models, combined with a multiplicative composition, predicts human AUT creativity ratings. Additive composition fails because it penalises long answers.
numbers: Study 1 N=171: latent multiplicative SD vs human ratings r=.91 (83% variance); additive factor r=-.37. Word count correlates -0.25 with SD but 0.41 with human ratings. Study 2: r=.75. Study 3 (brick): r=.45. Study 5 (1,856 noun responses): single models r=.76-.82 (CBOW ukwac .82, GloVe .77), rater alpha=.88.
limits: Correlations within sample and task; no criterion link for creative behaviour in Study 2. Latent variable inflates correlation vs a single observed score.
agent_relevance: Cheap code-level originality score exists. Handle the length bias: longer answers score lower on distance.

source: Beaty and Johnson (2021) Automating creativity assessment with SemDis
finding: Documents known limits of the AUT and its scoring: fluency has weak inter-item correlation, human ratings need trained raters and vary, and the task did not predict creative behaviour in one sample.
numbers: Inter-item fluency correlations on AUT as low as .3-.4 (Barbot 2018), up to .57-.71 in Forthmann 2017. Openness r=.57 with human ratings, r=.19 with SD in Study 3. Creative metaphor r=.39 with ratings, .20 with SD. Fluid intelligence and AUT ratings r=.26 (Beaty and Silvia 2012, cited).
limits: Secondary citations for those prior values.
agent_relevance: DT scores are weakly reliable at item level. Use many prompts.

source: Hass (2017), Baas et al. (2013), Nijstad et al. (2010) via Stevenson 2022 and Nath 2024: two-pathway theory of divergent thinking
finding: Creative ideas can arise by a persistent pathway (deep search in few concepts) or a flexible pathway (many category jumps); AUT shows more flexible switching than verbal fluency.
numbers: Not opened in primary form. Reported in Nath 2024: more jumps on AUT than animal fluency (p<0.001).
limits: Second-hand.
agent_relevance: Both routes are legitimate; operators for breadth and depth should both exist.

source: Runco (2008) Divergent thinking is not synonymous with creativity
finding: Cited by Stevenson 2022 as the argument that DT tests measure only one component of creativity. Not read directly.
limits: Not opened; only seen as a citation.
agent_relevance: Do not read DT metric as creative quality. Pair with value and evaluation.

source: Guilford (1950, 1967) Creativity; The nature of human intelligence (AUT)
finding: Guilford introduced divergent production and the Alternative Uses Test; AUT scored on fluency, flexibility, originality, elaboration. Stated in Stevenson 2022 and Haase 2023 as the origin of the task.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Not opened; description relies on secondary text.
agent_relevance: Fluency, flexibility, originality, elaboration give a four-part open-mode scorecard.

source: Silvia et al. (2008) subjective scoring and Mednick (1962) associative theory, as cited in Beaty and Johnson 2021 and the 2026 review
finding: Subjective top-2 / snapshot scoring on a 1-5 scale replaced uniqueness counts; Mednick links creativity to flatter associative hierarchies. Both only seen via citation.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Citation only.
agent_relevance: Associative flatness is the human analog of a high-entropy sampling distribution.
